sections.title: A Club Forms in 1908
sections.voiceover: It started with a club. In the autumn of 1908, white homeowners in Hyde Park formed the Hyde Park Improvement Protective Club. A prominent attorney named Francis Harper led it. Within a short time it counted 350 members, and the historian Allan Spear notes they included some of the wealthiest dwellers on the South Side. These were not fringe agitators. They were the lawyers, the businessmen, and the property owners who ran the neighborhood, and they had decided that Hyde Park would be a white neighborhood and would stay that way. A few hundred Black families had begun to settle near Lake Avenue. The club set out to undo that, block by block. The methods were not subtle. The club appointed a committee to buy up property owned by Black residents on white blocks. It offered cash bonuses to Black renters who would give up their leases and leave. And it threatened to blacklist any real estate firm that dared to sell or rent to a Black family across the line it had drawn. Within a couple of years the club itself faded, but it had already done its work. The small Black community along Lake Avenue shrank, and the rest of Hyde Park stayed white for the next forty years.

sections.title: Who the Wall Was Against
sections.voiceover: It is worth remembering who that wall was built against. One of the most prominent Black Chicagoans of these years was Fannie Barrier Williams. She had been the first Black woman admitted to the Chicago Woman's Club, a founder of Black women's organizations, and a writer who pressed the city and the nation to open its doors. She was exactly the kind of accomplished, settled, professional neighbor the club claimed it did not want. The color line did not ask what you had achieved. It asked only one question. To understand why white Hyde Park reacted with that much force, you have to look at what was happening to the city around it. The Great Migration was on. Across the South, Black families were leaving sharecropping, lynching, and Jim Crow, drawn north by wartime jobs in the packinghouses, the steel mills, and the rail yards. Many of them came up the Illinois Central line that ran straight into Chicago. The Chicago Defender, the city's great Black newspaper, fed the movement directly. Its publisher, Robert Abbott, printed train schedules and job listings and called for a Great Northern Drive in the spring of 1917. Pullman porters carried the paper south along the rail lines, and it was read aloud in barbershops and churches across the cotton country. Its circulation passed 125,000 by 1918.

sections.title: Into the Black Belt
sections.voiceover: Chicago's Black population grew from about 40,000 in 1910 to roughly 234,000 by 1930, and about 278,000 by 1940. Nearly seven times as many people in thirty years. They needed somewhere to live, and the city had decided in advance where that would be. Most newcomers were funneled into a narrow strip on the South Side that people called the Black Belt. It ran for miles north to south but was only a few blocks wide. Inside it, demand far outran supply, and landlords took full advantage. They chopped single apartments into tiny units called kitchenettes, sometimes a hundred square feet, with one bathroom and one stove shared down a hall. Six or seven families might crowd into a flat once leased to two. A Chicago Housing Authority study in the late 1930s found that nearly half of kitchenette tenants, about 45 percent, were paying more than 30 percent of their income just for rent. The sociologists St. Clair Drake and Horace Cayton, who mapped this world in their 1945 study Black Metropolis, described the same blocks holding several times the people they were built for. So Black families paid more, for less, and the color line was the reason. It left them nowhere else to go.

sections.title: The Answer Was a Bomb
sections.voiceover: When Black families did try to cross that line and rent or buy on a white block, the answer was often a bomb. From 1917 through 1919, roughly two dozen Black homes were bombed in Chicago. Between 1917 and 1920, on average, a Black-owned home or a real estate office that served Black buyers was bombed about once every twenty days. Almost none of the cases were ever solved, and no one went to prison for them. The pressure broke open in the summer of 1919. A Black teenager named Eugene Williams drifted across an invisible line in the water at a Lake Michigan beach. A white man threw rocks, one struck him, and he drowned. The police refused to arrest the white man witnesses named. What followed was a week of rioting. By the time it ended, 23 Black Chicagoans and 15 white Chicagoans were dead, more than 500 people were injured, and about a thousand Black families had lost their homes to arson.

sections.title: Jesse Binga Will Not Run
sections.voiceover: One man stood at the center of this storm and would not move. Jesse Binga came to Chicago in 1892, worked his way up from peddling and Pullman cars, and built a real estate fortune. In 1908 he opened the city's first Black-owned bank. In 1917 he bought a house at 5922 South Park Avenue, on a white block. His home and his offices were bombed at least five times between 1917 and 1921. He refused to leave. I will not run, he said, and he stayed. His story did not end in triumph. When the Depression hit, his bank, heavily invested in mortgages to Black churches and families, was shut down by the state in 1930. Binga lost everything, was convicted of embezzlement, and went to Joliet prison in 1935 at the age of 70. The same neighbors who had banked with him signed a petition for his release, and he was paroled in 1938 and pardoned in 1941. He died in 1950, largely forgotten, in the city he had helped build. His house still stands. Hold that picture in mind, a man who would not run from a bomb, because it shows what the next weapon was designed to avoid. There would be no more single defiant homeowners to rally around. The fight would move from the doorstep to the deed. After the riot, white Chicago reached for a quieter and more durable weapon than the bomb. The racially restrictive covenant. A covenant was a clause written into a property deed. It barred the owner from selling, leasing, or even allowing occupancy to anyone who was not white, with narrow exceptions for live-in servants.

sections.title: Signing in Blocs
sections.voiceover: One deed by itself did little. The power came from numbers. Neighbors signed in blocs, often pledging a set share of a block's frontage before the agreement took effect, so a single signed covenant could seal off whole streets at once. A standard printed form circulated so any block could adopt one. A Chicago attorney named Nathan MacChesney drafted a model covenant in 1927 that real estate boards handed out across the city. Beginning in the late 1920s, covenants swept across the white neighborhoods ringing the Black Belt, including Kenwood, Oakland, Hyde Park, Woodlawn, and Englewood. By the 1940s, hundreds of subdivisions across Cook County carried them. And the University of Chicago was not a bystander to this. From 1933 to 1947, the university spent more than 110,000 dollars on what it politely called community interests. More than 83,000 of those dollars went specifically to defending restrictive covenants in the blocks around its campus. The Chicago Defender had a blunter name for the whole arrangement. The paper called the covenants the University of Chicago Agreement to get rid of Negroes. The covenants were rarely beaten head-on, because the law was on their side. The Hansberry family came closest. Carl Hansberry, a real estate man himself, bought a home at 6140 South Rhodes Avenue in Woodlawn in the spring of 1937 and moved his family in that June. His daughter Lorraine was a young child. A white neighbor, Anna Lee, and the Woodlawn Property Owners Association went to court to enforce a covenant and drive the family out. A mob gathered outside. A brick came through a window and nearly struck Lorraine. The fight went all the way to the Supreme Court. In Hansberry versus Lee, decided November 12, 1940, the Court ruled in the family's favor. But it ruled on a narrow procedural point, namely that an earlier lawsuit could not legally bind him. It did not touch the covenants themselves, and it did not say they were unconstitutional. Lorraine Hansberry would later turn the family's ordeal into the play A Raisin in the Sun.

sections.title: Shelley v Kraemer 1948
sections.voiceover: The covenants finally fell in 1948, and the decisive case came not from Chicago but from St. Louis. In Shelley versus Kraemer, decided May 3, 1948, the Supreme Court held that a court could not enforce a racially restrictive covenant, because using the power of the courts to do so counted as state action barred by the Fourteenth Amendment. Chief Justice Fred Vinson wrote for the Court, which ruled six to nothing, with three justices stepping aside. The decision did not erase the racist clauses from the deeds. Many of those words sit in Chicago property records to this day. Shelley only made them unenforceable, so a judge could no longer evict a Black family for living where the deed said it must not. After 1948, Black families finally began crossing into Hyde Park and Kenwood. The line that the club had drawn in 1908 had held for forty years. Now it broke. But the people who had spent decades and dollars holding that line did not simply give up. They looked for new instruments that the courts would still permit. Zoning. Land clearance. Federal money. The same university that had funded the covenant defense was already thinking about what to do once the covenants were gone. The bomb had failed. The deed had failed. What came next would be quieter, larger, and backed by the full weight of the government, and it would reshape these blocks far more than any club ever could. That is the story of the chapter that follows.
